title: ElGamal
body:
[[Diffie-Hellman]] turned into an actual encryption scheme, 1985. The observation is small: run the
key exchange with yourself as one of the two parties, and use the shared value as a one-time mask.

Public parameters $p$ and $g$ as before. Bob's private key is $x$; his public key is $h = g^x$.

```
encrypt m:              decrypt (c1, c2):
  pick random k           s = c1^x = g^(kx)
  c1 = g^k                m = c2 * s^-1
  c2 = m * h^k
     = m * g^(xk)
```

Bob recovers $s$ because $c_1^x = (g^k)^x = g^{kx} = h^k$, the same value the sender used, and
inverting $s$ in $\mathbb{Z}_p^*$ is the extended [[Euclidean Algorithm]]. Recovering $m$ without
$x$ is the computational Diffie-Hellman problem, so the security assumption is the
[[Discrete Logarithm Problem]] one, not factoring.

Two properties fall straight out of the shape:

- **It is randomised.** A fresh $k$ per message means the same plaintext encrypts differently every
  time, so ElGamal has semantic security for free where textbook [[RSA]] has to bolt padding on.
  The cost of that is a **2× ciphertext expansion**: two group elements per message.
- **$k$ must never be reused.** Two messages under the same $k$ share $s$, so $c_2/c_2' = m/m'$ and
  one known plaintext gives the other. Exactly the [[Stream Cipher]] keystream-reuse failure in
  multiplicative clothing, and the same mistake later killed Sony's PS3 signing key through
  ElGamal's signature cousin, DSA.

ElGamal encryption is rarely deployed directly; the elliptic-curve integrated encryption scheme
(ECIES) is the modern form, and the **signature** variant is what became DSA. See
[[Digital Signature]].
